text:
Persistent application knowledge

Six months later, the platform should reconstruct what the application is, why it exists, how it works, who owns it, where it runs, and what has changed.

Identity and purpose

- Application name, description, business problem, intended outcomes, status, and criticality.
- Users, stakeholders, owners, support contacts, funding source, and organizational context.
- Scope, exclusions, assumptions, constraints, success measures, and complexity classification.

Requirements and decisions

- Approved functional and nonfunctional requirements, user journeys, business rules, and acceptance criteria.
- Key decisions, alternatives considered, rationale, approvers, approval dates, exceptions, and accepted risks.
- Backlog items, delivered scope, deferred work, known limitations, and technical debt.

Design and implementation

- Architecture, components, data models, integrations, dependencies, technology choices, and design artifacts.
- Source repositories, branches, build configuration, dependency versions, generated artifacts, and traceability from requirements to implementation.
- Security model, roles, permissions, data classifications, privacy controls, retention rules, and compliance obligations.

Testing and delivery

- Test strategy, results, unresolved defects, accessibility findings, performance evidence, security assessments, and user acceptance.
- Environment inventory, configuration references, deployment pipeline, release history, migrations, rollback procedures, and production approvals.
- The exact application version deployed in each environment and the commit, build, configuration, and database schema associated with it.

Operations and evolution

- Service objectives, monitoring, alerts, dashboards, runbooks, backup and recovery arrangements, and support model.
- Incidents, problems, vulnerabilities, patches, maintenance activity, usage trends, costs, and outcome measurements.
- A chronological audit trail showing who changed what, when, why, and under which approval.

Retention principles

- Store durable facts and artifacts as versioned records with provenance, timestamps, ownership, and confidence rather than relying only on conversation transcripts.
- Separate the historical build-time snapshot from current operational state, and identify when current facts were last verified.
- Retain links or authorized retrieval references for large artifacts; do not place passwords, access tokens, or unnecessary personal data in conversational memory.
- Apply access control, retention schedules, legal holds, deletion rules, and audit logging consistently.
- When answering later, cite the relevant version and explicitly flag stale, missing, conflicting, or unverified information.
limitations: The platform’s actual persistence, retrieval, retention, and access-control capabilities are unspecified.
